extracted.intended_audience: Researchers (authors) and potential peer reviewers planning to publish or review on Wellcome Open Research, particularly Wellcome-funded researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and criteria describing the open, post-publication peer review model used by Wellcome Open Research: who may review, what reviewers should assess, how reports are handled and published, and the status/approval rules that determine when an article has 'passed' peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal, invited, fully open peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Our peer review process is formal, invited, and fully open (meaning the reports are published alongside the article, along with reviewer names and affiliations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports and reviewer names/affiliations are published alongside the article to prioritise openness, transparency and collaborative conversation; openness reduces potential for bias and tends to make reports more constructive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review takes place after the article has been published openly on the platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing first and then conducting peer review balances faster dissemination with maintaining research integrity — research can be read and used while experts assess it, reducing delays that make findings outdated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers assess quality and validity of the research
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers are asked to assess the quality and validity of the research – so null and negative studies are welcome and won’t be reviewed any differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should focus on whether analysis is accurately presented and conclusions are justified and supported by the content of the article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review applied to all article types
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is applied to all article types, not just Research Articles; Method Articles, Software Tool Articles, Data Notes, etc. undergo the same open, post-publication peer review process as Research Articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This ensures readers can trust underlying work across a range of outputs and encourages publication of non-traditional outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewing allowed (training and inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: We offer the chance for co-reviewing, where early career researchers can work alongside a more senior researcher to review an article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-reviewing supports training of early career researchers and expands the pool of reviewers while maintaining oversight by a senior reviewer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must suggest at least five potential reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: After the article is accepted, authors need to suggest five possible reviewers. Our in-house editorial team will check your suggested reviewers and ensure they meet our criteria, and suggest any additional reviewers as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should provide five potential reviewers before publication; the editorial team will vet suggestions for suitability and conflicts of interest and may add reviewers if necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collaborative reviewer identification (authors + editorial team)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors and our editorial team collaborate to identify reviewers, rather than editors solely leading the process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors' subject expertise helps identify reviewers best placed to assess the work, but collaboration with editors is used to balance potential conflicts of interest and bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and conflict-of-interest considerations for reviewer selection
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s important to think about the diversity of your suggested peer reviewers: Are they from different institutions? Are they from different countries? Is there a good gender balance? This also needs to be balanced with potential conflicts of interest and possibilities for bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the five names you provide aren’t diverse enough, the editorial team may ask for more suggestions. Authors should avoid suggesting reviewers with conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer invitation and communications handled by editorial staff
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain integrity of the process, all communication with reviewers will come from our editorial staff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial staff formally invite reviewers once the article is live; if reviewers decline or miss deadlines, authors and editors will work together to suggest replacements and repeat invitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer Code of Conduct compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When reviewers submit their reports, they are checked by our editorial team to ensure they meet our reviewer Code of Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reports must adhere to the Code of Conduct (e.g., professional, constructive). Once confirmed, reports are published openly alongside the article with reviewer names and affiliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved status definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Approved — The article is of an appropriate academic standard. The analysis is accurately presented, and the conclusions are justified and supported by the content of the article. The reviewer may suggest small changes to improve the article or correct minor errors, but these changes will not affect the peer review status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An 'Approved' rating indicates the article meets academic standards; suggested minor edits do not block passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approved with reservations status definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Approved with reservations — The reviewer believes the article has academic merit but has asked for several small changes to the article or more significant revisions. The reviewers have made it clear that the changes requested are necessary for an ‘Approved’ status to be awarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This status signals necessary revisions that authors should address to achieve full approval; multiple such reports may still contribute toward passing as described in passing criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not approved status definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Not approved — The article in its current form has issues that seriously undermine the findings and conclusions. More serious revisions will be required for the paper to pass peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Not approved’ is not equivalent to rejection; authors can revise and submit a new version and repeat the peer review process to improve status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passing criteria for peer review and indexing
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the article has received two Approved ratings, or one Approved and two Approved with reservations, the article passes peer review and is indexed in industry databases such as Scopus and PubMed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are strongly encouraged to address reviewer feedback by commenting on the reports and publishing new versions; if the article does not obtain these approvals authors can revise and resubmit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended methods for finding reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Top tips for finding reviewers: Use your knowledge of the field to identify possible reviewers at relevant institutions; Try the Reviewer Finder Tool provided by Wellcome Open Research; Look at your references — authors of cited papers could be well-placed to review for you; Explore academic databases like PubMed or Scopus for recent articles with relevant keywords.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These approaches can help authors compile diverse, relevant reviewer suggestions to meet the five-reviewer requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on responding to reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Be thorough in responses: Address each point in turn and provide a full response, including an explanation of any changes made to the paper in light of the comment. Feel empowered to say no — you do not always need to agree with your reviewers and should feel empowered to say no, where you feel appropriate, providing a detailed explanation and further evidence if needed. Be prepared for multiple rounds of review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough, point-by-point responses build transparency and credibility; disagreements should be justified clearly and can be an opportunity to supply more evidence or explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: No bias against null or negative studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Null and negative studies are welcome on Wellcome Open Research and won’t be reviewed any differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers should assess quality and validity regardless of outcome; the platform supports dissemination of non-significant results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open reports and reader commenting to enable collaborative conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Open reports and open reader commenting enables collaborative conversation and an opportunity for learning across the full research community, not just between authors and reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing reports and allowing reader comments fosters transparency, wider learning, and may improve review quality and accountability.
